label: Lesson 3
title: The photoelectric effect
summary: When light strikes a metal surface, electrons can be ejected. The rules this follows, and Einstein’s photon explanation of them, were decisive evidence that light has a particle nature as well as a wave nature.

intro.text: The wave theory was hugely successful, but one experiment refused to fit it. Shine light on a clean metal surface and electrons fly off. This is the *photoelectric effect*, and the detailed rules it obeys are impossible to explain with waves alone.
The effect opened the quantum chapter of physics. This lesson sets out the observations, Einstein’s explanation, and the way the effect ties directly into wave-particle duality.

intro.title: The problem in one line
intro.body: The photoelectric effect depends on the *frequency* of the light, not its intensity, and the electrons appear instantly. Neither fact fits a model of light as a continuous wave.

sections.title: Threshold frequency and instantaneous emission
sections.summary: Electrons are ejected only above a threshold frequency, and they appear at once; brighter light ejects more electrons, but not more energetic ones.
keyPoints: Below a threshold frequency f0 no electrons are ejected, however intense the light.
Above the threshold, increasing the intensity increases the number of electrons, not their energy.
Emission is instantaneous, within about 10^-9 s, once the threshold is reached.
These rules clash with a wave picture, in which energy would build up gradually.

blocks.text: Shine light on a clean metal surface and, if the light is energetic enough, electrons are released. Measure them carefully and several rules emerge, all of them surprising from a wave point of view.

items: *Threshold frequency*: below a certain minimum frequency f0, no electrons are emitted at all, no matter how bright the light.
*Intensity sets numbers, not energy*: above the threshold, a brighter light produces more electrons, but each electron carries the same energy.
*Instantaneous*: the electrons appear the moment the light strikes the surface, within about 10^-9 s.

blocks.text: The wave picture predicts the opposite on both counts. A more intense wave delivers more energy, so a brighter light should eventually free electrons even at low frequency, given time to build up. And the energy should accumulate gradually, so emission should lag behind the light. Neither happens.

blocks.title: What actually controls the energy
blocks.body: In the photoelectric effect the energy of the ejected electrons depends on the *frequency* of the light, and the *number* of electrons depends on the intensity. Frequency and intensity play entirely separate roles.

sections.title: Einstein’s explanation
sections.summary: Einstein treated light as photons: a single photon is absorbed by a single electron, and its energy must first pay the work function before any is left as kinetic energy.
keyPoints: Light arrives as photons of energy hf, and one photon is absorbed by one electron.
The work function Φ is the minimum energy needed to remove an electron from the metal.
Energy conservation gives hf = Φ + KE_max.
An electron gains kinetic energy only from the surplus above the work function.

blocks.text: In 1905 Einstein explained the effect by taking the quantum idea seriously. Light is not a continuous wave when it interacts with matter: it arrives as photons, each of energy hf. A single photon is absorbed by a single electron in a single, localised event.

Every metal holds its electrons with some minimum binding energy, called the *work function* Φ. Before an electron can escape, the incoming photon must supply at least that much energy. Whatever is left over becomes the electron’s kinetic energy.

blocks.alt: Two panels: on the left a photon with energy below the work function cannot free an electron, and on the right a photon with energy above the work function frees an electron with the leftover energy as kinetic energy.
blocks.caption: The photoelectric effect. A photon frees an electron only if its energy **hf** exceeds the work function **φ**; the electron leaves with the leftover energy, KE = hf − φ.

blocks.text: This one equation explains every observation. If hf is below Φ, the photon cannot free an electron at all, which is the threshold. Above it, the surplus hf − Φ becomes kinetic energy, so the electron energy rises with frequency. Raising the intensity adds more photons and so more electrons, but each still carries only hf − Φ. And absorption is a single instant, so emission is instantaneous.

blocks.title: Maximum kinetic energy of a photoelectron
blocks.given: Light of wavelength 250 nm falls on a metal whose work function is 2.2 eV. Find the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons. Take h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s, and 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
steps: Subtract the work function: KE = hf − φ = 4.97 − 2.2 = 2.77 eV.
blocks.result: The fastest electrons leave with about 2.8 eV, or 4.4 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, of kinetic energy.

blocks.title: Reading the equation
blocks.body: The work function Φ is a property of the metal, for example about 1.95 eV for caesium. Light of a given frequency delivers a fixed photon energy hf. The equation says that the electron keeps the difference, no matter how intense the beam.

sections.title: Photocurrent and stopping potential
sections.summary: The stopping potential is the voltage that just halts the most energetic electrons; measuring it gives the maximum kinetic energy directly.
keyPoints: A photocurrent flows when ejected electrons are collected at an anode.
A reverse voltage can oppose them; the stopping potential V0 is the voltage that just stops the fastest electrons.
The maximum kinetic energy is KE_max = e V0.
Below the threshold frequency no current flows at any voltage.

blocks.text: To measure the electron energies, arrange the ejected electrons to cross an evacuated tube to a collecting electrode. A current flows. Now apply a reverse voltage to push the electrons back, and increase it until the current just falls to zero.

That critical voltage is the *stopping potential* V0. It measures the kinetic energy of the *fastest* electrons, because they are the last to be stopped. Since the potential energy gained by a charge e crossing a voltage V0 is eV0, the maximum kinetic energy is found from the stopping potential alone.

blocks.tex: KE_{max} = e V_0 \qquad\qquad e V_0 = h f - \Phi
blocks.caption: The stopping potential and the work function

blocks.alt: A graph of stopping potential against frequency: a straight line of slope h over e that crosses the horizontal axis at the threshold frequency f-zero.
blocks.caption: Stopping potential against frequency. The graph is a straight line of slope **h/e**; it crosses the axis at the threshold frequency **f₀**, where **hf₀ = φ**.

blocks.text: Plotting the stopping potential against the frequency of the light gives a straight line whose slope is h/e and whose intercept gives Φ. This was one of the first measurements to yield a value of the Planck constant, and it agreed with the value found from black-body radiation.

blocks.title: What the graph shows
blocks.body: The stopping-potential graph is a straight line that crosses zero at the threshold frequency f0. Below f0 there is no current at all; above it the line rises with slope h/e, independent of the metal. Only the intercept, the work function, changes from one metal to another.

sections.title: Why the photoelectric effect matters
sections.summary: The photoelectric effect proved that light interacts with matter as discrete quanta, laying the groundwork for wave-particle duality.
keyPoints: A single photon interacts with a single electron, with energy transferred in one localised event.
Threshold frequency and instantaneous emission cannot be explained by a continuous wave.
The effect shows that light carries energy in quanta of size hf.
It was a direct step towards wave-particle duality and the de Broglie hypothesis.

blocks.text: The photoelectric effect is more than a curiosity. It showed that, whatever light does while it travels, it exchanges energy with matter in discrete packets. A single photon strikes a single electron, and the energy is handed over in one localised event, not spread across a wave.

That is why the threshold and the instantaneity are decisive. A wave would share its energy over the whole surface and take time to build enough to free an electron; a photon either has enough energy or it does not, and it delivers it at once.

blocks.title: The groundwork for duality
blocks.body: The photoelectric effect forced physics to accept that light is both wave and particle. It led directly to the de Broglie hypothesis, that particles too have a wavelength, which the next lesson develops.

blocks.text: Downstream, the same physics is used every day. Photomultipliers and photodiodes rely on it to detect light, and photoelectron spectroscopy uses it to measure the electronic energy levels of materials. In this sense the effect is not only a founding experiment but a working tool.

questions.question: Below the threshold frequency, no electrons are emitted no matter how intense the light is. This shows that:
options: Brighter light has more energy per photon
Photon energy depends on frequency, not intensity
questions.explanation: Intensity changes the number of photons, not the energy of each one. Below the threshold no individual photon has enough energy to free an electron, however many arrive.

questions.question: Increasing the intensity of light above the threshold increases the energy of each ejected electron.
questions.explanation: Intensity increases the number of electrons ejected, but each electron’s energy is set by the frequency. Only frequency changes the electron energy.

questions.question: Above the threshold frequency, increasing the light intensity increases:
options: The kinetic energy of each electron
The number of electrons emitted per second
questions.explanation: More intense light means more photons per second, so more electrons are ejected. Their individual energy depends only on the photon energy hf and the work function.

questions.question: In the photoelectric effect, emission is essentially instantaneous once the threshold frequency is reached.
questions.explanation: Emission happens within about 10^-9 s. A single photon is absorbed by a single electron at once, so no time is needed to accumulate energy.

questions.question: In Einstein’s picture of the photoelectric effect, one photon is absorbed by:
questions.explanation: The interaction is one photon with one electron, a single localised event. This one-to-one transfer is what makes the effect depend on photon energy rather than intensity.

questions.question: The work function Φ of a metal is:
options: The energy of the incident light
The minimum energy needed to remove an electron from the metal
The kinetic energy of the ejected electron
questions.explanation: The work function is the minimum energy required to liberate an electron from the metal surface. The photon must supply at least this much before any electron is freed.

questions.question: Einstein’s photoelectric equation is:
questions.explanation: The photon energy hf is divided between the work function Φ and the maximum kinetic energy: hf = Φ + KE_max.

questions.question: A photon of energy 5.0 eV strikes a metal with work function 2.0 eV. What is the maximum kinetic energy of the ejected electron, in eV?
Light of frequency 1.0 × 10^15 Hz strikes a metal of work function 3.0 × 10^-19 J. What is the maximum kinetic energy of an ejected electron, in joules? Take h = 6.626 × 10^-34 J s.
Which statements about the photoelectric effect are correct? Select all that apply.
options: A photon transfers its energy to a single electron
The photon energy must exceed the work function to free an electron
The excess energy becomes the electron’s kinetic energy
Brighter light lowers the work function
questions.explanation: Absorption is one photon to one electron, and the photon energy must exceed the work function; the surplus becomes kinetic energy. Intensity does not change the work function.

questions.question: The stopping potential is the reverse voltage that:
options: Just stops the fastest emitted electrons
questions.explanation: The stopping potential is the reverse voltage at which the photocurrent falls to zero, because even the most energetic electrons can no longer reach the collector.

questions.question: The maximum kinetic energy of the ejected electrons is given by:
questions.explanation: An electron of charge e crossing a potential difference V0 gains energy eV0. So the stopping potential directly measures the maximum kinetic energy: KE_max = eV0.

questions.question: A photoelectric experiment gives a stopping potential of 1.5 V. What is the maximum kinetic energy of the electrons, in eV?
questions.explanation: KE_max = eV0; with V0 = 1.5 V, the maximum kinetic energy is 1.5 eV.

questions.question: A plot of stopping potential against frequency is a straight line whose slope is independent of the metal used.
questions.explanation: The slope is h/e, a universal constant. Only the intercept, which gives the work function, differs from one metal to another.

questions.question: If the frequency of the light is below the threshold frequency, the photocurrent at any applied voltage is:
questions.explanation: Below the threshold no photons have enough energy to free an electron, so no electrons are emitted and the current is zero regardless of the voltage.

questions.question: The photoelectric effect is strong evidence that light:
options: Interacts with matter in discrete quanta
questions.explanation: Because energy is transferred one photon at a time, the effect shows that light interacts with matter in discrete quanta of size hf, a particle-like property.

questions.question: Which observations of the photoelectric effect cannot be explained by a continuous wave model? Select all that apply.
options: The existence of a threshold frequency
The dependence of electron number on intensity
The independence of electron energy from intensity
questions.explanation: A threshold frequency, instantaneous emission, and electron energy independent of intensity all need the photon picture. A wave model does predict that more intensity means more energy and so more electrons.

questions.question: The photoelectric effect led towards the idea of wave-particle duality.
questions.explanation: By showing that light behaves as particles when it exchanges energy with matter, the effect forced physics to accept both wave and particle descriptions.

questions.question: Why does increasing the intensity of light below the threshold frequency free no electrons, however long you wait?
options: each photon still carries less energy than the work function, so no single photon can free an electron
the light is all reflected away
questions.explanation: Intensity means more photons, not more energetic ones. Freeing an electron needs a single photon with energy at least equal to the work function φ. Below the threshold, not one photon is energetic enough.

questions.question: Once light above the threshold frequency strikes a clean metal surface, electrons appear almost instantly.
questions.explanation: Emission is not a slow build-up of absorbed energy. One sufficiently energetic photon frees one electron straight away, so there is no measurable delay even in very faint light.

questions.question: A metal has a work function of 2.0 eV. Light delivers photons of energy 3.5 eV. Find the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons, in eV.
questions.explanation: The photon gives its energy to the electron. The work function φ is spent escaping the surface, so KE = hf − φ = 3.5 − 2.0 = 1.5 eV.

questions.question: The work function of a metal is the:
options: energy needed to remove an electron from its surface
energy of the brightest photon it can absorb
total energy of all its electrons
questions.explanation: The work function φ is the minimum energy needed to lift one electron out of the metal. Only photons with hf ≥ φ can start the process.

questions.question: Light of frequency 8.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz falls on a metal whose threshold frequency is 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Find the stopping potential, in volts. Take h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
questions.explanation: The extra energy above the threshold is h(f − f₀) = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ × (3.0 × 10¹⁴) = 1.99 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, which equals eV₀. So V₀ = 1.99 × 10⁻¹⁹ / 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 1.24 V.

questions.question: Which observations are evidence for the particle nature of light? Select all that apply.
options: there is a threshold frequency below which no electrons are emitted
the stopping potential depends on frequency rather than intensity
questions.explanation: A threshold, instant emission, and a stopping potential set by frequency all point to light arriving in discrete packets of energy. Diffraction is a wave effect and is evidence for the wave picture.

questions.question: The threshold frequency is:
options: the minimum frequency that ejects electrons from a metal
the maximum frequency the metal can absorb
the frequency at which the current is zero
questions.explanation: Below the threshold frequency no electrons are emitted, however intense the light; at or above it, emission begins.

questions.question: Below the threshold frequency, increasing the intensity of the light:
questions.explanation: Intensity changes how many photons arrive, not how much energy each carries. If no single photon has enough energy, no emission occurs.

questions.question: Photoelectric emission is instantaneous because:
options: a single photon can transfer all its energy to one electron at once
the electrons heat up slowly until they escape
questions.explanation: A photon is absorbed whole by one electron, so escape is immediate, with no build-up time.

questions.question: The threshold frequency depends on:
options: the work function of the metal
the area of the metal surface
questions.explanation: Each metal needs a minimum photon energy, hf₀, to free an electron, so the threshold is set by the metal's work function.

questions.question: Below the threshold frequency, no photoelectrons are emitted no matter how intense the light is.
questions.explanation: Intensity only adds more photons of the same energy. If each photon lacks the energy to free an electron, none is emitted.

questions.question: The wave theory predicts a delay before emission with dim light, but emission is observed to be immediate.
questions.explanation: If energy were gathered continuously from the wave, weak light would need time to accumulate. The observed instantaneity is a clue to the photon picture.

questions.question: Which statements about the threshold are correct? Select all that apply.
options: below it no electrons are emitted
it depends on the light intensity
questions.explanation: The threshold is set by the metal and marks the onset of emission, which is immediate above it. Intensity does not change the threshold.

questions.question: A metal has a work function of 2.0 eV. Find its threshold frequency in hertz. Take 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J and h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.
A metal has a work function of 3.0 eV. Find its threshold wavelength in nanometres. Use hc = 1240 eV·nm.
Einstein's photoelectric equation is:
questions.explanation: The photon brings energy hf, the electron pays the work function φ to escape, and the rest is its maximum kinetic energy.

questions.question: The work function φ of a metal is:
options: the minimum energy needed to remove an electron from the surface
the kinetic energy of the emitted electron
the energy of the incident photon
questions.explanation: The work function is the energy barrier an electron must overcome to escape the metal.

questions.question: Increasing the frequency of light above the threshold:
options: increases the maximum kinetic energy of the electrons
increases the number of electrons emitted
questions.explanation: Higher frequency means more energetic photons, so the electrons leave with more kinetic energy. The number of electrons is set by intensity.

questions.question: Above threshold, increasing the intensity increases the number of photoelectrons but not their maximum kinetic energy.
questions.explanation: More intense light delivers more photons per second, so more electrons are freed, but each photon has the same energy, so KEmax is unchanged.

questions.question: In the simple photoelectric picture, one electron can absorb energy from several photons at once.
questions.explanation: The process is a one-photon, one-electron event. That is why a low-frequency photon cannot free an electron no matter how many arrive.

questions.question: According to Einstein's equation, KEmax depends on which of the following? Select all that apply.
options: the work function of the metal
questions.explanation: KEmax = hf − φ depends on the photon frequency and the metal's work function. Intensity and photon number affect how many electrons, not how energetic.

questions.question: Light of frequency 8.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz strikes a metal of work function 2.0 eV (3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ J). Find KEmax in joules. Take h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.
The stopping potential is:
options: the reverse voltage that just stops the photocurrent
the work function expressed in volts
questions.explanation: Applying a reverse voltage decelerates the electrons; at the stopping potential even the fastest electrons fail to reach the collector.

questions.question: The stopping potential V₀ is related to the maximum kinetic energy by:
questions.explanation: The work done against the stopping voltage, eV₀, just cancels the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons.

questions.question: A graph of stopping potential against frequency is a straight line whose slope is:
questions.explanation: Since eV₀ = hf − φ, dividing by e gives V₀ = (h/e)f − φ/e, so the slope is h/e.

questions.question: The intercept of the stopping-potential graph on the frequency axis gives:
questions.explanation: V₀ falls to zero at the threshold frequency, where the photon energy just equals the work function.

questions.question: The stopping potential depends on the frequency of the light, not on its intensity.
questions.explanation: Intensity changes the size of the photocurrent, but the maximum kinetic energy, and hence the stopping potential, is set by the frequency.

questions.question: The slope of the stopping-potential against frequency graph is the same for all metals.
questions.explanation: The slope is h/e, a universal constant, so every metal gives a line of the same slope but a different intercept.

questions.question: From a graph of stopping potential against frequency, one can determine: Select all that apply.
options: the work function of the metal
questions.explanation: The slope gives h/e (hence h), and the intercepts give φ and f₀. Intensity is not read from this graph.

questions.question: A metal has a threshold frequency of 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Find its work function in electronvolts. Take h = 4.14 × 10⁻¹⁵ eV s.
In a photoelectric experiment, light of wavelength 400 nm falls on a metal of work function 2.0 eV. Find KEmax in electronvolts. Use hc = 1240 eV·nm.
questions.explanation: Photon energy = 1240/400 = 3.1 eV. Then KEmax = 3.1 − 2.0 = 1.1 eV.

questions.question: The photoelectric effect is direct evidence that light:
options: delivers its energy in discrete packets
questions.explanation: The existence of a threshold and the instantaneous emission show that energy arrives in whole photons.

questions.question: Which observation is impossible to explain with the wave theory of light?
options: no emission below the threshold frequency
questions.explanation: A continuous wave should eventually supply enough energy at any frequency; the sharp threshold is the giveaway of quantised energy.

questions.question: Which device makes direct use of the photoelectric effect?
options: a solar cell and a photodetector
questions.explanation: Solar cells and photodetectors turn light into a current by freeing electrons with photons.

questions.question: Above threshold, the photocurrent is proportional to:
questions.explanation: Each photon frees at most one electron, so more photons per second (higher intensity) means more electrons per second.

questions.question: Which change increases the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons?
questions.explanation: Only a higher photon frequency raises KEmax. Intensity, area and distance change the number of electrons, not their energy.

questions.question: The photoelectric effect shows that light has particle as well as wave properties.
questions.explanation: The wave picture explains interference and diffraction, while the photoelectric effect reveals the photon, so both pictures are needed.

questions.question: Einstein explained the photoelectric effect using the idea of photons.
questions.explanation: Building on Planck's quanta, Einstein treated light as packets of energy hf, which accounted for the threshold and the kinetic-energy relation.

questions.question: Bright light of sufficiently high frequency ejects more electrons per second than dim light of the same frequency.
questions.explanation: More intense light delivers more photons per second, so more electrons are freed each second.

questions.question: Which facts support the photon picture of light? Select all that apply.
options: the existence of a threshold frequency
KEmax depends on frequency, not intensity
questions.explanation: The threshold, the instantaneity and the frequency dependence of KEmax all point to quantised energy. Bending at a boundary is ordinary refraction.

questions.question: A metal has a work function of 4.0 eV. Find the minimum frequency of light, in hertz, that can cause emission. Take h = 4.14 × 10⁻¹⁵ eV s.
Photons of energy 4.0 eV strike a metal of work function 1.5 eV. Find the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons, in electronvolts.
questions.explanation: KEmax = hf − φ = 4.0 − 1.5 = 2.5 eV.
